1. college.edu starts its web server, which **binds** to port 443 and waits.
2. Aisha's browser picks a free ephemeral port, 51520, for this connection.
3. It sends a segment to 203.0.113.10:443 with 192.168.1.42:51520 as the source.
4. The server's operating system sees port 443 in the header and hands the data to the web server, not the mail server.
5. The reply is addressed back to port 51520, so Aisha's OS hands it to the browser and not the music app.

![Ports and sockets — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/ports-and-sockets/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **a port is something physical, like the socket you plug a cable into**. Actually, **a** port is just a number in the segment header. Nothing physical exists.

The confusion is made worse by the word "socket", which in networking means an IP-and-port pair, not a hole in a wall. Nothing is opened or plugged in. The operating system simply keeps a list saying "port 443 belongs to this program", and reads the number off each arriving segment.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "What is a port?" and "What is a socket?" Often followed by "which port does HTTPS use?"

Model answer:

A port is a 16-bit number in the transport header that identifies which program on a machine the data is for. The IP address gets the packet to the machine; the port gets it to the right process. Ports 0 to 1023 are well-known and fixed by convention, like 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH and 53 for DNS. Clients use random high-numbered ephemeral ports for their side of a connection. A socket is an IP address and port together. A connection is actually identified by four values source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port which is how one machine can hold many simultaneous connections to the same server.

subject: CN
title: TCP vs UDP
summary: Not every application wants the same thing. Two very different needs exist.
notes:
When a web page loses a piece, you want it sent again. When a video call loses a piece, sending it again is pointless — that moment has already passed.

## Why & what

**Why there are two protocols.** Not every application wants the same thing. Two very different needs exist.

- Some data must be **complete**. A missing line of code in a downloaded file makes it useless.
- Some data must be **current**. A video frame that arrives two seconds late is worse than no frame at all.

You cannot serve both with one protocol, so the transport layer offers two.

**What TCP is. TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) is **connection-oriented and reliable**.

- It agrees a connection first, with a handshake.
- It numbers every byte, so pieces can be reassembled in order.
- It waits for acknowledgements and resends anything that goes missing.
- Its header is 20 bytes.

**What UDP is. UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is **connectionless and unreliable**.

- No handshake. It just sends.
- No numbering, no reordering, no acknowledgements, no resending.
- Its header is 8 bytes — source port, destination port, length, checksum. That is all.

"Unreliable" is a technical word here, not an insult. It means makes no promises, not works badly.

The comparison, in the order interviewers ask for it:

|  | TCP | UDP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection | handshake first | just send |
| Lost data | detected and resent | gone forever |
| Order | reassembled in order | arrives however |
| Speed | slower, more checking | faster, no checking |
| Header | 20 bytes | 8 bytes |
| Used by | HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP | DNS, video calls, games, DHCP |

## How it works

How an application chooses.

1. Ask: is late data still useful? If yes, TCP. If no, UDP.
2. Aisha loading college.edu — every byte matters, and a page half a second late is fine. **TCP.**
3. Aisha on a video call with Rahul — a frame from two seconds ago is useless. Skipping it is better than stalling. **UDP.**
4. A DNS lookup one tiny question, one tiny answer. Setting up a whole TCP connection would cost more than just asking again if it fails. **UDP.**
5. The choice is made by the application when it opens the socket. The network does not decide.

![TCP vs UDP — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/tcp-vs-udp/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **UDP is just a worse, broken version of TCP**. Actually, **UDP is deliberately** minimal, and for live traffic that is the better design.

Imagine a video call using TCP. One frame goes missing, so TCP stops and waits for the resend before delivering anything after it. Your call freezes for half a second, then jumps. Everything that arrived on time was held back for something that no longer mattered. UDP just skips the missing frame. You see one tiny glitch and the call keeps flowing.

TCP's reliability is a cost, paid willingly when it is worth it.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Difference between TCP and UDP?" probably the single most asked networking question in placements. Give the table, then give a reason for each side.

Model answer:

TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. It sets up a connection with a three-way handshake, numbers the data, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits what is lost, and delivers everything in order. Its header is 20 bytes. UDP is connectionless. It sends datagrams with no handshake, no acknowledgements, no ordering and no retransmission, with an 8-byte header. The choice depends on whether late data is still useful. Web pages, file transfers and email use TCP because completeness matters. Video calls, gaming and DNS use UDP because speed matters more than perfection — retransmitting an old video frame would stall the stream for data that is already useless.

subject: CN
title: The three-way handshake and connection teardown
summary: TCP promises ordered, reliable delivery. To keep that promise, both sides must agree on things before data starts flowing.
notes:
Before Aisha's browser sends a single byte of her request, three messages have already gone back and forth. That round trip is a real part of why the first load of a site feels slower than the rest.

## Why & what

**Why a handshake is needed.** TCP promises ordered, reliable delivery. To keep that promise, both sides must agree on things before data starts flowing.

- Is the other side actually there and listening?
- What number will each side start counting from?
- Both sides need to confirm they can send **and** receive.

What the pieces are.

- **SYN** a flag in the TCP header meaning "synchronise". It means: I want to start, and here is my starting number.
- **ACK** — a flag meaning "acknowledge". It means: I received up to here.
- **Sequence number (seq)** — where this side's counting begins.
- **Acknowledgement number (ack)** the next byte number this side expects to receive.

The starting sequence number is deliberately random, not zero, to make it hard for an attacker to guess and inject fake segments.

**Why closing takes four steps.** A TCP connection is full duplex — two independent streams, one in each direction. Each direction must be shut separately, because Aisha finishing her upload does not mean the server has finished sending the page.

## How it works

Opening three messages.

1. Aisha sends **SYN**, seq=100. Meaning: I want to talk, my numbering starts at 100.
2. The server replies **SYN + ACK**, seq=500, ack=101. Meaning: I agree, my numbering starts at 500, and I am ready for your byte 101.
3. Aisha sends **ACK**, ack=501. Meaning: got yours, ready for your byte 501.

The connection is now open, and the HTTP request goes out.

Closing — four messages.

4. Aisha sends **FIN**, the server replies **ACK**. Her direction is now closed, but the server can still send.
5. The server sends its own **FIN**, Aisha replies **ACK**. Both directions closed.

![The three-way handshake and connection teardown — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/the-three-way-handshake-and-connection-teardown/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the three-way handshake carries the request itself**. Actually, **the handshake** carries no application data at all. It is pure setup.

Aisha's GET /results goes out as a fourth message, after the handshake completes. That is why the handshake costs a full round trip before anything useful is sent, and why protocols like QUIC were designed to cut it down.

A related mix-up: the middle step is one message, not two. SYN and ACK are two flags set in the same segment, which is why it is three-way and not four-way.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Explain the three-way handshake" and the follow-up "why does closing take four steps?" Being able to answer the second one separates you immediately.

Model answer:

To open a connection, the client sends a SYN with its initial sequence number. The server replies with SYN plus ACK in a single segment — its own initial sequence number, and an acknowledgement of the client's. The client sends a final ACK. Three messages, and now both sides know the other can send and receive, and both know the starting sequence numbers.

Closing takes four because a TCP connection is full duplex, so each direction closes independently. One side sends FIN and gets an ACK, which closes that direction only. The other side keeps sending until it is finished, then sends its own FIN and gets an ACK. No application data travels in the handshake. It costs one full round trip before the first request goes out.

subject: CN
title: How TCP stays reliable
summary: Recall Module 4: the data link layer detects a damaged frame and silently drops it. Nobody is told. Recall Module 5: IP forwards packets and makes no promise they arrive. A router with a full queue simply discards them.
notes:
The internet loses packets constantly. Right now, somewhere on Aisha's path, one just vanished. She will never notice.

## Why & what

**Why reliability has to live here.** Recall Module 4: the data link layer detects a damaged frame and silently drops it. Nobody is told. Recall Module 5: IP forwards packets and makes no promise they arrive. A router with a full queue simply discards them.

So by the time data reaches the transport layer, loss has already happened and nobody below has done anything about it. TCP is the first layer that notices and reacts.

What the three tools are.

- **Sequence numbers.** Every byte TCP sends is numbered. The receiver can spot gaps and put out-of-order pieces back in order.
- **Acknowledgements.** The receiver sends back the number of the next byte it expects. ACK=3 means "I have everything before 3, send me 3."
- **Retransmission timer.** The sender starts a timer for each segment. No acknowledgement before the timer expires means the segment is assumed lost and sent again.

TCP acknowledgements are **cumulative**: ACK=5 confirms everything up to byte 4, not just byte 4.

## How it works

1. The server sends segments seq=1, seq=2, seq=3, seq=4. Each starts a timer.
2. Segments 1 and 2 arrive. Aisha's laptop replies ACK=3 — I have 1 and 2, send me 3.
3. Segment 3 is dropped by a busy router. Segment 4 arrives anyway.
4. Aisha's laptop cannot acknowledge 4, because 3 is still missing. It repeats ACK=3.
5. The server's timer for segment 3 expires, or it sees the repeated ACKs, and resends segment 3. Once it arrives, Aisha's laptop jumps straight to ACK=5.

Three duplicate ACKs in a row triggers an immediate resend without waiting for the timer. That is **fast retransmit**.

![How TCP stays reliable — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/how-tcp-stays-reliable/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the receiver sends a message saying which segment was lost**. Actually, **the** receiver only ever says what it is waiting for next.

There is no "please resend segment 3" message in TCP. The receiver keeps answering ACK=3, and the sender works out the rest. This is a small design choice with a big effect: the receiver stays simple, and even if some ACKs are lost themselves, the next one still carries the full picture, because ACKs are cumulative.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "How does TCP guarantee reliable delivery?" Say all three tools, not just retransmission.

Model answer:

TCP numbers every byte it sends with a sequence number, so the receiver can reorder segments that arrive out of order and detect gaps. The receiver acknowledges data by sending back the sequence number of the next byte it expects. Acknowledgements are cumulative, so one ACK confirms everything before that number. The sender keeps a timer for unacknowledged data. If it expires, the segment is retransmitted. If the sender receives three duplicate ACKs, it retransmits immediately without waiting — that is fast retransmit. The receiver never names the missing segment. It just keeps repeating the number it is waiting for, and the sender infers the loss.

subject: CN
title: Flow control and congestion control
summary: The receiver stores arriving data in a buffer — a chunk of memory — until the application reads it. If data arrives faster than the application reads it, the buffer fills, and anything more is dropped.
notes:
Two completely different things can force a sender to slow down. The receiver cannot keep up. Or the network in between cannot keep up. Students merge these two constantly. Interviewers know that.

## Why & what

**Why flow control exists.** The receiver stores arriving data in a **buffer** — a chunk of memory — until the application reads it. If data arrives faster than the application reads it, the buffer fills, and anything more is dropped.

A fast server can easily overwhelm a slow laptop. So the receiver needs a way to say "slow down, I am full."

**What flow control is. Flow control** stops the sender from overwhelming the **receiver**.

The receiver puts a **window size** in every ACK it sends: the number of bytes of free buffer space it has left. The sender may not have more than that unacknowledged at any moment. This is the **sliding window**.

If the buffer fills completely, the receiver advertises a window of zero, and the sender pauses.

**What congestion control is. Congestion control** stops the sender from overwhelming the **network**.

The receiver may be perfectly fine while a router halfway along the path has a full queue and is dropping packets. No router sends a complaint. So the sender has to guess, using the only signal it has: **lost packets mean congestion**.

The sender keeps a second window, the **congestion window**, which it manages itself.

- **Slow start** begin small, and double the window every round trip. Despite the name, it grows very fast.
- **Congestion avoidance** — after a threshold, grow by one segment per round trip instead of doubling.
- **On loss** — cut the window sharply and build up again.

That grow-slowly, cut-sharply pattern is called **AIMD** (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease). It is what keeps the internet from collapsing when everyone browses at once.

## How it works

1. Aisha's laptop advertises a receive window in every ACK — say, 64 KB free.
2. The server also keeps its own congestion window, starting small and doubling each round trip.
3. Before sending, the server takes **the smaller of the two windows**. That is how much unacknowledged data it may have in flight.
4. If a segment is lost, the server treats it as congestion, cuts its congestion window, and slows down.
5. As ACKs keep arriving cleanly, the window grows again, and the speed climbs back up.

![Flow control and congestion control — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/flow-control-and-congestion-control/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **flow control and congestion control are two names for the same thing**.

Actually, **they solve different problems and get their information in opposite ways.**

- Flow control protects **the receiver**. The receiver tells the sender its window in every ACK. It is explicit.
- Congestion control protects **the network**. No router tells the sender anything. The sender infers trouble from packet loss. It is a guess.

One is a stated limit. The other is a guessed limit. The sender always obeys whichever is smaller at that moment.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Difference between flow control and congestion control?" The examiner is specifically checking whether you can separate them.

Model answer:

Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. The receiver advertises a window size in every acknowledgement, showing how much free buffer space it has, and the sender keeps its unacknowledged data within that. If the buffer fills, it advertises a zero window and the sender pauses. Congestion control prevents the sender from overwhelming the network itself. No router reports congestion, so TCP infers it from packet loss. The sender maintains a congestion window, growing it exponentially during slow start, then linearly during congestion avoidance, and cutting it sharply on loss. That is additive increase, multiplicative decrease. The key difference is scope and signal: flow control is about the receiver and is explicitly advertised, congestion control is about the network in between and is inferred. The sender sends the minimum of the two windows.

subject: CN
title: DNS
summary: Packets can only be addressed to numbers. But people cannot remember numbers, and the numbers change — a college can move hosting and get a new IP tomorrow.
notes:
Aisha typed college.edu. Every module since has used 203.0.113.10. Nobody has explained who did the swap.

## Why & what

**Why DNS exists.** Packets can only be addressed to numbers. But people cannot remember numbers, and the numbers change — a college can move hosting and get a new IP tomorrow.

So we need a phone book. But a single phone book for the whole internet is impossible.

- It would be enormous.
- It would change thousands of times a second.
- Every lookup on earth would hit one machine.

The answer is to split it up, and let each organisation keep its own small piece.

**What DNS is. DNS** (Domain Name System) turns a name into an IP address, using a tree of servers where each one knows only its own part.

The parts of results.college.edu, read **right to left**:

- . — the root, at the far right, usually invisible
- edu — the **TLD** (Top Level Domain)
- college — the domain
- results — a subdomain or host

The players.

- **Resolver** — the server that does the work for you, usually run by your ISP or a public one like 8.8.8.8. Aisha's laptop got its address from DHCP.
- **Root servers** — know which server handles each TLD.
- **TLD servers** — know which server handles each domain in that TLD.
- **Authoritative server** — actually owns the answer for that domain.

**Record types worth knowing: A** (name to IPv4), **AAAA** (name to IPv6), **CNAME** (this name is an alias for that one), **MX** (mail server for this domain), **NS** (which server is authoritative).

## How it works

1. Aisha's browser checks its own cache, then the operating system's cache. If either has college.edu, it stops here.
2. Otherwise it asks the resolver at 8.8.8.8: what is the address for college.edu?
3. The resolver asks a **root** server. Root replies: I do not know, but the .edu servers do — here they are.
4. The resolver asks the **.edu** server. It replies: I do not know, but ns.college.edu is authoritative — here it is.
5. The resolver asks ns.college.edu, gets 203.0.113.10, caches it, and returns it to Aisha.

DNS normally uses **UDP on port 53**, because the exchange is one small question and one small answer. Setting up a TCP connection would cost more than simply asking again if the reply goes missing.

![DNS — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/dns/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the DNS server fetches the web page**. Actually, **DNS only returns an address.** It never touches the page.

The two are completely separate conversations. First Aisha's laptop talks to 8.8.8.8 over UDP port 53 and receives twelve bytes of answer. That connection ends. Only then does it open a brand new TCP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 443 and ask for the page.

DNS is directory enquiries. It gives you the number and hangs up.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "How does DNS work?" and "Does DNS use TCP or UDP?" The second is a trap — the honest answer has a "but".

Model answer:

DNS maps domain names to IP addresses using a hierarchy of servers, so no single machine has to store the whole internet. The client asks a resolver. If the resolver has no cached answer, it queries a root server, which points it to the TLD servers for .edu. The TLD server points to the authoritative server for that domain, which returns the actual A record. The resolver caches the result and returns it. DNS uses UDP on port 53 for normal lookups, because a query and reply are small and retrying is cheaper than a handshake. It falls back to TCP for large responses and for zone transfers between servers. Caching happens at every level — browser, operating system and resolver — so most lookups never reach the root at all.

subject: CN
title: DHCP
summary: Every device needs four settings before it can do anything useful: an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway and a DNS server.
notes:
Aisha connects to HostelNet-3F for the first time. Two seconds later she has an IP address, a mask, a gateway and a DNS server. She typed none of them.

## Why & what

**Why DHCP exists.** Every device needs four settings before it can do anything useful: an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway and a DNS server.

Setting those by hand would mean the warden configuring forty laptops, keeping a register so nobody gets a duplicate address, and redoing it every time a student leaves. Unworkable.

**What DHCP is. DHCP** (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) hands out those settings automatically when a device joins a network.

The four settings together are called a **lease**, because they are borrowed for a fixed time, not owned. When Aisha leaves for the holidays, her lease expires and the address goes back into the pool for someone else.

The four messages: DORA.

- **D**iscover — is any DHCP server out there?
- **O**ffer — yes, you can have this address.
- **R**equest — I will take it.
- **A**cknowledge — it is yours, for this long.

DHCP runs over UDP, on **port 67 for the server** and **port 68 for the client**.

## How it works

1. Aisha's laptop joins the Wi-Fi with no IP address at all. It broadcasts a **DISCOVER** to 255.255.255.255, because it cannot address anyone specifically yet.
2. The DHCP server — inside the hostel router — replies with an **OFFER** of 192.168.1.42, plus the mask, gateway and DNS server.
3. Her laptop broadcasts a **REQUEST**, formally accepting that offer.
4. The server sends an **ACK** confirming the lease and its duration, and marks the address as taken so nobody else is offered it.
5. Partway through the lease, her laptop quietly asks to renew. If she stays all term, she keeps the same address the whole time.

![DHCP — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/dhcp/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the third message is unnecessary — why request what was already offered?** Actually, **REQUEST exists because there might be more than one DHCP server.**

If two servers hear the DISCOVER, Aisha receives two OFFERs. She broadcasts her REQUEST naming which one she accepted, so the winning server marks the address as taken and the losing server puts its offer back in the pool. Without that step, addresses would be reserved and never claimed.

A second small mix-up: DISCOVER is broadcast because Aisha has no address yet. She cannot address a specific server, and cannot be replied to directly.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Explain DHCP" or "What is the DORA process?" Naming all four steps and what the lease contains is the full-marks answer.

Model answer:

DHCP automatically assigns network configuration to a device when it joins. It uses four messages, known as DORA. The client broadcasts a Discover, because it has no address yet. A server replies with an Offer containing a candidate IP address. The client broadcasts a Request accepting one specific offer, which matters when multiple DHCP servers responded. The server sends an Acknowledge confirming the lease and its duration. The lease includes the IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server address — not just the IP. Leases are time-limited and renewed automatically, so addresses return to the pool when devices leave. It runs over UDP, port 67 on the server side and 68 on the client side.

subject: CN
title: HTTP and HTTPS
summary: TCP delivers a stream of bytes. It has no idea what those bytes mean.
notes:
Everything so far has been delivery — addresses, routes, ports, acknowledgements. None of it said what Aisha actually wants. That sentence is HTTP.

## Why & what

**Why HTTP exists.** TCP delivers a stream of bytes. It has no idea what those bytes mean.

Both sides need an agreed way to say "give me the results page" and "here it is, and it is HTML, and it is 60 KB". That agreement is HTTP.

**What HTTP is. HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the language browsers and web servers speak. It is plain text, and simple enough to read by eye.

A **request** has:

- a **method** — GET to fetch, POST to send data, PUT to update, DELETE to remove
- a **path** — /results
- **headers** — extra information, like Host: college.edu

A **response** has:

- a **status code** — 200
- **headers** — like Content-Type: text/html
- a **body** — the actual page

Status codes, by first digit:

| Family | Means | Common example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2xx | it worked | 200 OK |
| 3xx | look somewhere else | 301 Moved Permanently |
| 4xx | your mistake | 404 Not Found |
| 5xx | the server's mistake | 500 Internal Server Error |

**HTTP is stateless.** The server remembers nothing between requests. Each one arrives with no memory of the last. Cookies exist precisely to work around that — the browser sends a small token back each time so the server can recognise the same user.

**What HTTPS is. HTTPS** is exactly the same HTTP, wrapped inside **TLS** encryption, on port 443 instead of 80.

TLS does three things:

- **Encryption** — nobody in between can read the contents.
- **Identity** — a **certificate**, signed by a trusted authority, proves the server really is college.edu.
- **Integrity** — tampering in transit is detected.

## How it works

1. TCP is already connected — that was the handshake in Topic 6.3.
2. For HTTPS, a TLS handshake runs next: the server presents its certificate, both sides agree on keys.
3. Aisha's browser sends the request: GET /results HTTP/1.1, with Host: college.edu.
4. The server finds the page and replies with 200 OK, headers, and the HTML body.
5. The browser reads the HTML, spots images and stylesheets it needs, and sends more requests for those — often reusing the same connection.

![HTTP and HTTPS — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/http-and-https/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **HTTPS is a different protocol from HTTP**. Actually, **HTTPS is the identical** protocol, running inside an encrypted tunnel.

The methods are the same, the headers are the same, the status codes are the same. Change nothing but the port and the wrapper. This also explains what HTTPS does not hide. The routers along the path still see Aisha's IP address, the server's IP address, and the port. They cannot see the path she asked for, the headers, or the page. The envelope is sealed; the address on the outside is still readable.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Difference between HTTP and HTTPS?" and "What does 404 mean?" — plus the strong follow-up "what does stateless mean?"

Model answer:

HTTP is the request-response protocol between a browser and a web server. A request carries a method like GET or POST, a path, and headers. A response carries a status code, headers and a body. Status codes group by first digit: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error like 404 Not Found, 5xx server error. HTTP is stateless — the server keeps no memory between requests, which is why cookies and sessions exist. HTTPS is the same protocol carried inside TLS on port 443. TLS gives encryption, integrity, and server identity through a certificate. Someone watching the traffic still sees which IP addresses are talking, but not the URL path, the headers or the content.

subject: CN
title: Full trace, end to end
summary: Every module so far explained one stage in isolation. Interviews ask for the whole thing, in sequence, in about ninety seconds.
notes:
Aisha opens her laptop and loads college.edu. You now know every single thing that happens. This topic just puts them in order.

## Why & what

**Why this topic exists.** Every module so far explained one stage in isolation. Interviews ask for the whole thing, in sequence, in about ninety seconds.

Nothing here is new. If any stage feels unfamiliar, that is a signal to reread that module rather than memorise this list.

The fixed cast, one last time.

- aisha-laptop — 192.168.1.42, MAC AA:BB:CC:11:22:33
- Hostel router **HostelNet-3F** — 192.168.1.1 inside, 103.21.58.7 outside, MAC DD:EE:FF:00:11:22
- ISP **AirLink** — next hop 103.21.58.1
- Resolver — 8.8.8.8
- college.edu — 203.0.113.10, port 443

## How it works

The whole journey, grouped into five stages.

1. **Join the network.** DHCP's DORA exchange gives her 192.168.1.42, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 8.8.8.8. (Module 7)
2. **Find the address.** Her browser asks 8.8.8.8 for college.edu over UDP 53. Root, then .edu, then the authoritative server. Answer: 203.0.113.10. (Module 7)
3. **Decide where to send it.** 203.0.113.10 AND the mask does not match her own network, so it goes to the gateway. She ARPs for 192.168.1.1, gets DD:EE:FF:00:11:22, and builds an Ethernet frame. (Modules 4 and 5)
4. **Cross the internet.** The router NATs her source to 103.21.58.7:40001, matches the default route 0.0.0.0/0, and forwards to AirLink. Each router along the way strips the frame, reads the IP header, and builds a new frame for the next hop. (Modules 4 and 5)
5. **Talk to the server.** TCP three-way handshake to port 443, TLS handshake, then GET /results. The response comes back as numbered segments, acknowledged and reassembled, and the browser draws the page. (Modules c and 7)

![Full trace, end to end — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/full-trace-end-to-end/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the IP addresses change as the packet crosses each router**. Actually, **the** MAC addresses change at every hop. The IP addresses stay the same end to end.

This is the single most useful idea in the course, and it is worth stating precisely.

- **MAC addresses** answer "who is the next device on this wire?" They are rewritten at every single hop.
- **IP addresses** answer "who is the final destination?" They stay put.

The one exception is NAT, which deliberately rewrites the source IP at the boundary — and that is exactly why NAT is considered a special case rather than normal routing.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "What happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?" The most common networking interview question there is. Ninety seconds, in order, no rambling.

Model answer:

First the machine needs to be on the network at all — DHCP gives it an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server. The browser resolves the domain name using DNS, checking its cache, then the OS cache, then a resolver, which walks the root, TLD and authoritative servers over UDP port 53. With the IP address, the host ANDs it with its subnet mask, finds the destination is not local, and so sends it to the default gateway. It uses ARP to find the gateway's MAC address and builds an Ethernet frame. Each router strips the frame, reads the IP header, applies longest prefix match, and builds a new frame for the next hop — so MAC addresses change every hop while the IP addresses stay the same. NAT rewrites the source address at the network boundary. At the server, TCP completes a three-way handshake on port 443, TLS negotiates encryption, and the browser sends an HTTP GET. The response comes back as segments, which TCP reorders and acknowledges, and the browser renders the page.

subject: CN
title: Wi-Fi basics
summary: A cable is a private corridor. Radio is a room where everybody can hear everybody.
notes:
Aisha's Wi-Fi is fine at her desk and useless in the corridor. Nothing about the network changed. Only the distance did.

## Why & what

**Why wireless is a different problem.** A cable is a private corridor. Radio is a room where everybody can hear everybody.

That one difference causes the rest.

- Every nearby device competes for the same air.
- Any device in range receives your signal, meant for them or not.
- Walls and distance weaken it, so speed drops as you walk away.

What the words mean.

- **SSID** — the network's name, announced constantly by the access point. HostelNet-3F is one.
- **Band** — which slice of radio spectrum is used: 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz.
- **Channel** — a narrower slot inside a band. Two nearby APs on the same channel interfere.
- **CSMA/CA** — Carrier Sense Multiple Access with **Collision Avoidance**, the rule for taking turns.

The two bands.

|  | 2.4 GHz | 5 GHz |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reaches | further | shorter distance |
| Speed | slower | faster |
| Through walls | better | poorly |
| Crowding | busy | much quieter |

**Why CA and not CD.** Wired Ethernet used CSMA/**CD** — Collision Detection. A device could listen while transmitting and notice a clash.

A radio cannot. Its own transmission drowns out everything else. So Wi-Fi avoids collisions instead: listen first, and if the air is busy, wait a random moment and retry.

## How it works

1. The access point broadcasts its SSID so devices know it is there.
2. Aisha's laptop associates and authenticates with the password.
3. Both sides agree encryption keys — WPA2 or WPA3 on any modern network.
4. Before sending, her laptop listens. If the air is busy, it waits a random moment.
5. When clear, it sends. Everything after this is identical to a cable: same frames, same IP packets.

![Wi-Fi basics — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/wi-fi-basics/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **5 GHz is simply better than 2.4 GHz**. Actually, **5 GHz is faster but travels less** far and is stopped more easily by walls.

At her desk, 5 GHz wins easily. Two walls away in the corridor, 2.4 GHz may be the only band still working. In radio, faster and further are a trade-off, not a ranking.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?" This is the wireless question that actually gets asked.

Model answer:

Wired Ethernet could detect collisions because a device can listen on the wire while transmitting. A radio cannot — its own transmission is far stronger than anything it would hear, so collisions are undetectable at the sender. So Wi-Fi avoids them instead: sense whether the channel is idle, wait a random backoff if busy, then transmit. The other differences follow from radio being shared everyone in range competes for the air and everyone in range receives the signal, which is why WPA2 or WPA3 is standard rather than optional.

subject: CN
title: Common attacks
summary: The original protocols verify almost nothing.
notes:
Everything in this course assumed the packets were honest. Nothing in the design of IP or Ethernet actually checks that.

## Why & what

**Why attacks are possible at all.** The original protocols verify almost nothing.

- Nothing in an Ethernet frame proves the source MAC is real.
- Nothing in an IP header proves the source IP is real.
- Plain HTTP is readable by every device on the path.

Security was added later, on top. Understanding these attacks is mostly understanding what the original design left out.

The four you must know.

- **Sniffing** — quietly capturing traffic that was not meant for you. On old hubs this was trivial, because every port got a copy. On open Wi-Fi it is still possible, because radio reaches everyone.
- **Spoofing** — sending packets that claim to come from someone else's address. Possible because the source field is simply written by the sender, and nothing checks it.
- **Man in the middle (MITM)** — positioning yourself between two parties and relaying their traffic while reading it. Both sides think they are talking directly.
- **DDoS** (Distributed Denial of Service) — flooding a server with so much traffic from so many machines that real users cannot get through. Not a break-in. An overwhelm.

**What actually stops them.** Notice how short the list of defences is.

| Attack | What defeats it |
| --- | --- |
| Sniffingencryption — captured traffic is unreadable |  |
| Spoofing | verification — checks that confirm who really sent it |
| MITM | certificates — the identity check fails |
| DDoS | filtering and rate limits before the traffic arrives |

Three of the four come down to **encryption** or **proving identity**.

## How it works

Take MITM against Aisha, since it ties the whole course together.

1. An attacker on HostelNet-3F sends fake ARP replies claiming that 192.168.1.1 is at the attacker's MAC address.
2. Aisha's laptop believes it — recall from Topic 4.5 that ARP has no verification at all.
3. Her frames now go to the attacker instead of the router.
4. The attacker forwards them onward, so her browsing still works and nothing looks wrong.
5. If she is on plain HTTP, everything is readable. If she is on HTTPS, the certificate does not match and her browser shows a warning.

That last step is the whole reason certificates exist.

![Common attacks — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/common-attacks/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **a DDoS attack breaks into the server**. Actually, **it never gets inside anything.** It just makes the server too busy to answer.

Nothing is stolen or modified. The server does exactly what it was built to do, but so many requests arrive that real users get nothing. That is why its defences differ from every other attack here. Encryption does not help. Passwords do not help. Only filtering the flood before it arrives does.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "What is a man-in-the-middle attack?" or "Difference between DoS and DDoS?"

Model answer:

In a man-in-the-middle attack, an attacker places themselves between two communicating parties and relays traffic while reading or altering it, so both sides believe they are talking directly. On a local network this is often done by poisoning ARP, since ARP has no authentication. HTTPS defeats it, because the attacker cannot present a valid certificate for the domain. A DoS attack floods a target from one source; a DDoS uses many machines at once, which makes it far harder to filter by address and much harder to absorb. Neither is a break-in the goal is to exhaust capacity so real users cannot be served. Most of these are possible because the original protocols verify nothing. The general defences are encryption for confidentiality and certificates or authentication for identity.

subject: CN
title: Firewall, VPN and proxy
summary: Each solves a different problem. Home routers bundle all three, which is exactly why they get confused.
notes:
Three boxes that sit between you and the internet. Students name all three when asked about any one of them.

## Why & what

**Why they exist.** Each solves a different problem. Home routers bundle all three, which is exactly why they get confused.

**Firewall — decides what is allowed.** A **firewall** inspects traffic and permits or blocks it by rules: address, port, protocol or direction. Blocking all inbound traffic on port 22 is a firewall rule.

Modern firewalls are **stateful** — they remember that Aisha started a conversation, allow the reply, and block anything unsolicited.

**VPN — hides and relocates.** A **VPN** (Virtual Private Network) builds an encrypted tunnel from your device to a VPN server, and all traffic goes through it. The hostel network and AirLink see only encrypted traffic to one address. Websites see the VPN server's address, not 103.21.58.7. **Proxy — speaks on your behalf.** A **proxy** fetches things for you. Aisha asks the proxy, the proxy asks the website, the answer returns the same way, and the website sees the proxy. Unlike a VPN, a proxy usually covers one application and often encrypts nothing.

## How it works

1. Aisha's request leaves her laptop.
2. A **firewall** in the way decides by its rules whether the packet passes at all.
3. With a **VPN** on, the packet is encrypted and wrapped for the tunnel first, so the hostel network cannot see the destination.
4. With a **proxy** configured, her browser asks the proxy, and the proxy makes its own request to college.edu.
5. The reply returns through whichever were used, in reverse.

![Firewall, VPN and proxy — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/firewall-vpn-and-proxy/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **a VPN makes you anonymous**. Actually, **a VPN moves who can see you. It** does not remove them.

The hostel network and AirLink can no longer see where Aisha goes. The VPN provider now can every request passes through them, decrypted at their end. The website still knows it is being visited, still sets cookies, and still recognises her if she logs in.

A VPN shifts trust from your network operator to your VPN operator. Real benefit on untrusted Wi-Fi. Not invisibility.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Difference between a firewall, a VPN and a proxy?" Give the one-line version for each first, then a detail.

Model answer:

A firewall filters — it checks traffic against rules on address, port and protocol and allows or blocks it. Stateful ones track existing connections, so replies are allowed while unsolicited inbound traffic is not. A VPN encrypts — an encrypted tunnel to a VPN server, so the local network cannot see the destination and websites see the VPN's address. It covers all traffic from the device. A proxy substitutes — it requests on your behalf, so the destination sees the proxy.

Usually per-application, and often unencrypted. They are complementary, not alternatives.

subject: CN
title: Encryption basics and certificates
summary: Symmetric encryption uses one key to lock and unlock. Fast, good for bulk data. But both sides need the same key, and sending it over an untrusted network defeats the point.
notes:
Encryption makes Aisha's traffic unreadable. But unreadable to whom? If she is talking to an impostor, perfect encryption just means she is confiding in the wrong person very securely.

## Why & what

Why there are two kinds of encryption.

**Symmetric encryption** uses one key to lock and unlock. Fast, good for bulk data. But both sides need the same key, and sending it over an untrusted network defeats the point.

**Asymmetric encryption** uses a key pair. Anything locked with the **public key** opens only with the matching **private key**, so the public key can be handed to anyone. That solves the sharing problem, but it is slow.

**Real systems use both.** HTTPS uses asymmetric briefly, only to agree a shared symmetric key, then switches to symmetric for the data.

**Why certificates are needed.** Asymmetric encryption proves someone holds a private key. It does not prove who they are.

A **certificate** binds a public key to a domain name, signed by a **Certificate Authority (CA)** that browsers already trust. The signature says: this public key really does belong to college.edu. An attacker cannot get a CA to sign a certificate for a domain they do not control, so Aisha's browser warns her.

## How it works

1. Aisha's browser connects and the TLS handshake begins.
2. The server sends its certificate: public key, domain, and the CA's signature.
3. The browser checks that signature against the CA list it ships with, that the name matches, and that it has not expired.
4. If it passes, both sides use asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key.
5. Everything after that uses the fast symmetric key.

![Encryption basics and certificates — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/encryption-basics-and-certificates/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **the padlock icon means a website is safe**. Actually, **it only means the** connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the name.

A scam site can get a valid certificate for its own domain in minutes, and the padlock then looks identical to a real bank's. It guarantees two things: nobody is reading this in transit, and you are connected to the domain in the address bar. It says nothing about whether that domain deserves trust. Encryption protects the channel, not the other end of it.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** "Difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?" and "What is a digital certificate?"

Model answer:

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but distributing the key securely is the hard part. Asymmetric uses a public and private key pair — anything encrypted with the public key opens only with the private one, so the public key can be shared openly. It is much slower. HTTPS uses both: asymmetric during the TLS handshake to agree a session key, then symmetric for the data. A certificate binds a public key to a domain and is signed by a CA the browser trusts. That is what stops a man-in-the-middle substituting their own key — they cannot get a trusted CA to sign for a domain they do not control.

subject: CN
title: The master answer
summary: Why this one question. "What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?" is loved by interviewers because one question tests eight topics at once.
notes:
There is one question you will almost certainly be asked. You have already learned the whole answer. What is left is delivering it in order, without freezing.

## Why & what

**Why this one question.** "What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?" is loved by interviewers because one question tests eight topics at once.

It shows them whether you understand the layers as a connected system or as eight memorised definitions. Someone who really understands it narrates a journey. Someone who does not lists facts in random order.

**What a good answer looks like.** Six beats, in order, about ninety seconds total.

| Beat | What you say | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Get on the network — DHCP | 10s |
| 2 | Turn the name into a number — DNS | 15s |
| 3 | Local or remote — mask, then ARP | 15s |
| 4 | Cross the internet — NAT and routing | 20s |
| 5 | Connect and ask — TCP, TLS, HTTP | 20s |
| 6 | Receive and render | 10s |

**The rule for depth.** Depth is negotiable, order is not. If you are running long, shorten each beat. Never drop one.

Beat 1 is the one people skip, and it is free marks — most candidates start at DNS and never mention that the machine had to get an address first.

## How it works

The full answer, said out loud:

1. **"First the machine needs to be on the network."** DHCP's DORA exchange gives it an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server.
2. **"Then the name has to become an address."** The browser checks its cache, then the OS cache, then asks a resolver, which queries root, then the TLD, then the authoritative server. Answer: an A record. This is UDP on port 53.
3. **"Now, is that address local?"** The host ANDs the destination with its subnet mask. It does not match, so the packet goes to the default gateway. It uses ARP to find the gateway's MAC address and builds an Ethernet frame.
4. **"Crossing the internet."** NAT rewrites the private source address to the public one. The router matches the destination against its routing table using longest prefix match and forwards. Every hop strips the frame and builds a new one, so MAC addresses change while the IP addresses stay the same.
5. **"At the server."** TCP completes a three-way handshake on port 443, TLS negotiates encryption and validates the certificate, then the browser sends GET /results.
6. **"Coming back."** The response arrives as numbered segments, TCP acknowledges and reorders them, and the browser renders the page.

![The master answer — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/the-master-answer/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **a longer answer scores better**. Actually, **a complete answer scores better,** and length works against you.

An answer that spends ninety seconds on DNS alone and never reaches TCP looks worse than a ninety-second answer covering all six beats at moderate depth. The interviewer is checking for gaps, and a gap is invisible if you never got there.

Say all six. Then stop. If they want depth, they will ask — and a follow-up question you answer well is worth more than volunteering the same content unprompted.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** exactly the question above. Sometimes narrowed: "just the DNS part", or "what happens after the TCP connection opens".

**Model answer:** the six beats in section 3, spoken continuously. If you can say those without notes, this topic is done.

title: Rapid fire and the confusion table
summary: Interviewers use quick questions to calibrate. They are not looking for depth — they are checking whether the basics are automatic or whether you are reconstructing them each time.
notes:
The first two minutes of a networking round are usually short questions with short answers.

Hesitating on "which port is HTTPS" costs more than getting a hard question slightly wrong.

## Why & what

**Why rapid fire exists.** Interviewers use quick questions to calibrate. They are not looking for depth — they are checking whether the basics are automatic or whether you are reconstructing them each time.

Answers should take two seconds. Not because speed is impressive, but because hesitation on a definition suggests you learned it last night.

The facts that must be instant.

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Port for HTTP / HTTPS | 80 / 443 |
| Port for DNS / SSH / SMTP | 53 / 22 / 25 |
| Port for DHCP | 67 server, 68 client |
| Bits in IPv4 / IPv6 | 32 / 128 |
| Bits in a MAC address | 48 |
| Ethernet — MTU | 1500 bytes |
| TCP / UDP header size | 20 / 8 bytes |
| Usable hosts in a /26 | 62 |
| Router / switch / hub layer | 3 / 2 / 1 |
| PDU at network / data link layer | packet / frame |
| Layers in OSI / TCP-IP | 7 / 4 |
| Default route | 0.0.0.0/0 |

**The confusion table.** These ten are the Common Confusions from every module, in one place. Each one is a point where a weak answer and a strong answer diverge.

| From | Students say | Actually |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | internet = network | one network made of networks |
| M2 | a hub is a slow switch | a hub copies to every port |
| M3 | 7 layers means 7 programs | layers 7, 6 and 5 are usually one |
| M4 | MAC addresses reach anywhere | MAC is local, rewritten every hop |
| M5 | bigger prefix, bigger network | bigger prefix, smaller network |
| M5 | NAT is a firewall | NAT translates, never inspects |
| M6 | UDP is a broken TCP | UDP is deliberately minimal |
| M6 | flow control = congestion control | receiver vs network |
| M7 | DNS fetches the page | DNS returns an address, then stops |
| M8 | the padlock means the site is safe it | means encrypted, and the name matches |

## How it works

How to use this topic as practice.

1. Cover the answer column of the fact table. Say each answer out loud. Anything that takes more than two seconds goes on a list.
2. Do the same with the confusion table, but say the correction, not the mistake.
3. For any correction you cannot explain in one sentence, reread that module's Common Confusion section.
4. Repeat until both tables are automatic.
5. Then stop revising facts. Once these are instant, extra revision on them adds nothing put the time into 9.1 and 9.3 instead.

![Rapid fire and the confusion table — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/rapid-fire-and-the-confusion-table/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **rapid-fire answers should be padded out to sound thorough**. Actually, **a short** question wants a short answer, and padding reads as uncertainty.

Asked "which port does SSH use?", the answer is "22". Not "I think it is 22, though it can be configured differently, and some people move it to 2222 for security." All of that is true and none of it was asked. Answer the question, stop, and let them ask the follow-up. Volunteering caveats to a one-word question makes a confident fact sound like a guess.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** a burst of six to ten short questions with no pauses. The scoring is on hesitation as much as accuracy.

**Model answer:** the fact table above, said without thinking.

title: Mock drill and self-check
summary: Everything so far has been read. But interviews are spoken, and speaking exposes things reading hides — you lose your place, you use a word you cannot define, you realise mid-sentence that you do not actually know why ARP is needed.
notes:
Reading a model answer and saying one are different skills. The gap between them only closes by talking out loud, badly, several times.

## Why & what

**Why speaking is the missing practice.** Everything so far has been read. But interviews are spoken, and speaking exposes things reading hides — you lose your place, you use a word you cannot define, you realise mid-sentence that you do not actually know why ARP is needed.

Those failures are the point. Better to find them now.

**What the drill is.** Three rounds, about five minutes total. Do it with a friend, or into your phone's voice recorder.

- **Round 1 — rapid fire, 60 seconds.** Definitions and port numbers from 9.2, answered without pausing.
- **Round 2 — work it out, 3 minutes.** A subnetting question, solved out loud while you work. Split 192.168.1.0/24 into 8, or find which subnet 192.168.1.200/27 belongs to.
- **Round 3 — the trace, G0 seconds.** The full six-beat answer from 9.1, no notes.

Round 2 matters more than it looks. Interviewers who give you a subnetting problem are watching your method, not waiting for the number. Silence while you calculate tells them nothing. Narrating tells them everything.

## How it works

1. Record yourself doing all three rounds without stopping, even when you stumble. Stopping to restart hides the problem.
2. Play it back. Mark every place you paused for more than two seconds, and every term you used but could not have defined.
3. Each mark points at one module. Go back to that module, not to this one.
4. Redo the drill the next day, not the same hour. Sleep is what turns a reread into recall.
5. Stop when the recording is boring — steady, unhurried, no repair sentences.

**The self-check.** You are ready when you can do all five:

- trace the whole journey without looking anything up
- subnet a /24 into any number of pieces, out loud
- say which layer any device or protocol belongs to
- explain TCP vs UDP with a reason, not just a list
- name what changes at each hop, and what does not

![Mock drill and self-check — figure 1](/study-notes/cn/mock-drill-and-self-check/fig-1.png)

## Common confusion

Students think **more rereading is what fixes a shaky answer**. Actually, **rereading builds** recognition, and interviews test recall.

Rereading Module 5 makes subnetting feel familiar, which feels like progress. But familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the answer from nothing, and the difference only shows up when someone is watching.

One spoken attempt teaches you more about your gaps than three rereads. Do the drill badly first, then reread the specific thing that broke.

## Interview angle

**Asked as:** this topic is the practice, not a question. But the habit it builds — narrating your reasoning while you work — is scored in every technical round you will ever sit.

If you go blank in a real interview, say what you do know and work outward. "I know the destination is not local, so it has to go to the gateway — and to build the frame I need the gateway's MAC, which means ARP." Reasoning out loud from something certain is far better than silence, and interviewers frequently give partial credit for method alone.
